column2: Thus, Brahmins, four Manus are remembered as Meru-Savarnis; the past, the present and likewise the future ones —
the Manus have been declared to you by me just as I heard them. Now I shall tell of their sages, sons and groups of gods.
Marichi, Atri, the revered Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya and Vasishtha — these seven are the sons of Brahma.
In the northern direction too, Brahmins, are the seven sages; and Agnidhra, Agnibahu, Medhya, Medhatithi, Vasu,
Jyotishman, Dyutiman, Havya, Savala and Putra — these are the ten greatly mighty sons of Svayambhuva Manu.
This, Brahmins, is declared the first manvantara. Aurva, Vasishtha's son, Stamba, Kashyapa,
Prana, Brihaspati, Datta, Atri and Chyavana: these great sages, Brahmins, of great vows, were spoken of by Vayu.
The gods are remembered as the Tushitas in the Svarochisha interval; Havighna, Sukriti, Jyoti, Apa and Murti too are remembered,
Pratita, Nabhasya, Nabha and Urja: these are the sons of the great-souled Svarochisha Manu, Brahmins,
the earth-protectors of great strength and valour have been declared. This second manvantara has been told by me, Brahmins.
I shall tell of this third; understand it, best of Brahmins. There were seven sons of Vasishtha, known as the Vasishthas.
Of Hiranyagarbha (Brahma), the very radiant sons were born of Urja. The sages here have been named by me; listen to those now being recited.
These, best of sages, are the ten sons of Uttama Manu: Isha, Urja, Tanurja, Madhu, Madhava,
Shuchi, Shukra, Saha, Nabhasya and Nabha. The Bhanavas are the gods there; the manvantara is declared.
I shall now tell you the fourth manvantara: Kavya, Prithu, Agni, Jahnu and Dhata, best of Brahmins,
Kapivan and Akapivan: these are the seven sages there, Brahmins; sons and grandsons are recorded in the Purana, Brahmins,
and the hosts of gods, in the interval of Tamasa Manu: Dyuti, Tapasya, Sutapas, Tapobhuta, Sanatana,
Taporati, Akalmasha, Tanvi, Dhanvi and Parantapa: these are declared the ten sons of Tamasa Manu.
This fourth interval was spoken of by Vayu, best of sages. Devabahu, Yadudhra, the sage Vedashiras,
Hiranyaroma, Parjanya, Urdhvabahu, Somaja, Satyanetra and Atreya: these are the other seven sages;
and the gods are the Abhutarajasas, and the Prakritis are remembered; Varivlava and Raibhya — it is called the interval of the Manu.
Now understand these sons of his as I tell: Dhritiman, Avyaya, Yukta, Tattvadarshi, Nirutsuka,
Aranya, Prakasha, Nirmoha, Satyavak and Kriti are the sons of Raivata Manu; this is the fifth interval.
I shall tell the sixth; understand it, best of Brahmins. Bhrigu, Nabha, Vivasvan, Sudhama, Viraja,
Atinama and Sahishnu: these are the seven great sages. In the interval of Chakshusha Manu, Brahmins, these are remembered as the gods.
They are renowned from childhood, each separately, the dwellers in heaven; the Lekhas by name are remembered as five groups of gods.
Sons of the sage Angiras, great-souled and very mighty, the Nadvaleyas, best of sages, are famed as ten sons.
Ruru and the others, Brahmins, were in the interval of Chakshusha Manu. The sixth manvantara has been told; hear the seventh.
Atri, the revered Vasishtha, the great sage Kashyapa, Gautama, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra,
and likewise the revered son of the great-souled Richika, Jamadagni the seventh: these are the sages now in heaven.
The Sadhyas, Rudras, Vishvedevas, Vasus, Maruts, Adityas and the two Ashvins are remembered as the gods of Vaivasvata.
These belong to the present interval of Vaivasvata Manu, and the ten great-souled sons headed by Ikshvaku.
Of these great sages, of great might, who have been named, Brahmins, their sons and grandsons are in all directions.
In all manvantaras previously there were groups of seven, for the ordering of dharma in the world and the protection of the world.
When a manvantara has passed, four groups of seven, having done their work, go to heaven, to the untroubled world of Brahma.
Then others, endowed with austerity, fill that place; thus in succession, Brahmins, the past, the present
and the future seven great sages are remembered in heaven, having reached the interval of Savarni Manu here, Brahmins.
Rama (Parashurama), Vyasa, Atreya the radiant and very learned, Bharadvaja, and Drauni Ashvatthama of great splendour,
Gautama, Ajara, Gautama named Sharadvan, Kaushika, Galava, Aurva and Kashyapa —
these seven great-souled ones will be, best of sages. Vairi, Adhvarivan, Shamana, Dhritiman, Vasu,
Arishta, Adhrishya, Vaji and Sumati will be the sons of Savarni Manu, best of sages.
By rising at dawn and reciting these, a man prospers happily, gains great fame and becomes long-lived.
These manvantaras, seven and seven, have been truly told in brief, Brahmins; hear also the future ones.
There are five Savarni Manus, Brahmins; understand them: one is Vaivasvata, and four are of Prajapati.
Brahmins, the sons of Parameshthin have attained the name Meru-Savarni; they are the daughter's sons of Daksha, sons of Priya, kings,
endowed with great austerity, of great might, on the back of Meru. Raucya Manu is remembered as the son of the Prajapati Ruchi.
Bhautya, the son of Ruchi, was begotten on the goddess Bhuti. These seven are remembered as the future Manus in this kalpa.
By them this whole earth with seven continents and cities is to be protected for a full thousand yugas, best of Brahmins.
And the Prajapati by austerity constantly brings about dissolution in them; those yugas, a little more than seventy, have been declared;
joined with the Krita, Treta and other yugas, it is called the interval of a Manu. Fourteen Manus have been told, increasers of fame.
In the Vedas with the Puranas, all of them are mighty lords of beings, Brahmins; the recital of them is blessed.
In the manvantaras there are dissolutions, and at the ends of dissolutions, creations; their end cannot be told even in hundreds of years.
Of the creation of beings and the dissolution, Brahmins, in the manvantaras the dissolutions are heard of, best of Brahmins.
The gods remain there with a remainder, together with the seven sages, endowed with austerity, celibacy and learning.
When a full thousand yugas is complete, the kalpa is called finished; then all beings are burned by the rays of the sun.
Placing Brahma at the front, along with the hosts of Adityas, Brahmins, they enter the best of gods, the lord Hari-Narayana,
the creator of all beings, again and again at the ends of kalpas; the unmanifest, eternal God, whose is all this world.
Here I shall tell you, tigers among sages, of the creation of the present Vaivasvata Manu, of great splendour.
Here, in the course of the lineage, an ancient account is told, in which the great-souled lord Hari was born in the Vrishni family.
Thinking "this is a second Samjna (a double of Samjna)," Aditya (the Sun) then begot a son like himself on the second Samjna.
This one is like the Manu born earlier, the lord thought; he became a Manu by name and is called Savarna.
The second son of hers should be known as Shanaishchara (Saturn). The earthly Samjna, Brahmins, then
showed more affection to her own son, not so to the elder ones. Manu tolerated that of hers, but Yama did not bear it.
Out of anger, childishness, or the destined event, sinless one, Vaivasvata Yama threatened Samjna with his foot.
Then in anger the mother of Savarna cursed him, greatly pained: "This foot of yours shall fall."
But Yama, with joined palms, reported all that to his father, greatly agitated by fear of the curse, doubtful at Samjna's words.
May this curse be turned back, he said to his father, Brahmins; "a mother should behave with affection toward all her sons.
She, having cast us aside here, Vivasvan, wishes to favour (her own); my foot was raised against her but was not dropped on her body.
Out of childishness or fickleness or delusion, you should forgive it. I have been cursed, lord of the world, by my mother, O best of the burning; by your grace may my foot not fall, lord of rays."

Without doubt, son, there will be a great cause here, by which anger entered you, knower of dharma and speaker of truth.
brahmapuran:6:29	This word of your mother cannot be made false: worms will take the flesh and go to the ground.
brahmapuran:6:30	Your mother's word will thus be fulfilled, and by this counter to the curse you will be saved.
Aditya said to Samjna: "Why is affection for one son greater than for the others who are equal?"
She, avoiding that, did not tell Vivasvan; he, concentrating himself, saw the truth by yoga.
Wishing to curse her, the revered one did not curse, best of sages; he seized her by the hair.
Then she told Vivasvan everything as it had happened. Hearing that, Vivasvan, angry, went to Tvashtri.
Seeing him, Tvashtri duly honoured the Sun, who wished to burn him in anger, and then soothed him:

This form of yours, filled with excessive brilliance, does not look well, and Samjna, not bearing it, roams in the forest of grass.
brahmapuran:6:37	Today you will see your own well-conducted, praiseworthy wife endowed with yogic power, having taken to yoga, lord of rays.
brahmapuran:6:38	If it should be agreeable to you, god, with my consent, I shall fashion today a form of yours that is lovely, subduer of foes.
Then, upon consent, Tvashtri mounted Martanda Vivasvan on a lathe and trimmed away that brilliance, Brahmins.
Then the form, made luminous with its brilliance compressed, shone, lovelier than lovely to behold.
Taking to yoga, he saw his own wife in the form of a mare, unassailable by all beings through her radiance and her discipline.
Roaming fearlessly in a mare's body, Brahmins — the lord, in the form of a horse, approached her at the mouth.
She, struggling against intercourse out of suspicion of a stranger, expelled his seed through her nostrils.
Two gods were born of her, the Ashvins, best of physicians, remembered as Nasatya and Dasra, the two Ashvins.
These are the two sons of Martanda, the eighth Prajapati. Then the Sun showed her his lovely form.
Seeing her husband, she was delighted, best of sages. But Yama, his mind greatly pained by that action,
pleased these people with dharma; he, the Dharmaraja, of supreme radiance, gained through that good action
lordship over the ancestors and the position of world-guardian. Savarni became Manu, the Prajapati, rich in austerity.
When he arrives, in the Savarnika interval, he will become Manu; even today he constantly performs austerity on the back of Meru.
His brother Shanaishchara obtained the status of a planet. Tvashtri with that brilliance fashioned Vishnu's discus,
unobstructed in battle, with the intent of destroying the Danavas. The younger one, Yami, was a famed daughter,
and became the best of rivers, the Yamuna, purifier of the world. He is called Manu in the world and also Savarna.
The second son of that Manu, the brother Shanaishchara, obtained planethood, honoured by all the worlds.
The best of men who hears this birth of the gods, if fallen into calamity is freed, and gains great fame.
Anarta was his country and his city was Kushasthali. Raiva's son was Raivata, the righteous Kakudmi,
his eldest son. Having gained the kingdom at Kushasthali, with his daughter he went and heard music of the Gandharvas in Brahma's presence,
which to the god seemed a moment, Brahmins, but he stayed many yugas. He then returned to his city, now filled with Yadavas,
made into Dvaravati, many-gated and lovely, guarded by Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, led by Vasudeva.
There, Raivata, knowing the truth, best of Brahmins, gave that daughter Revati, called Subhadra, to Baladeva,
and went to the peak of Meru, established in austerity. Rama, righteous-souled, also lived happily with Revati.

Great-minded one, how, when a time of many yugas had passed, did old age not reach Revati and Raivata Kakudmin,
brahmapuran:7:36	or how did Sharyati's line remain on the earth even today, after he had gone to Meru? We wish to hear the truth.

Neither old age, hunger or thirst, nor death, best of sages, affects them; the cycle of seasons prevails in Brahma's world always, sinless ones; and Kakudmin went to the heavenly world after Raivata had gone.
That Kushasthali, Brahmins, was seized by Punyajana Rakshasas. The righteous, great-souled one had a hundred brothers.
Struck by the Rakshasas, they fled in all directions, Achyutas; and of those fleeing hundred brothers, best of Brahmins,
a very great lineage arose here and there, best of Brahmins; these, best of sages, are famed as the Sharyatas.
They are Kshatriyas endowed with virtue, famed in all directions; the greatly mighty ones entered every impenetrable place.
Two sons, Nabhaga and Arishta, vaishyas, attained Brahmin status; from Karusha came the Karushas, Kshatriyas, intoxicated by war.
Prishadhra, having killed his teacher's cow, best of Brahmins, fell into shudra status by a curse. These nine are declared.
The sons of Vaivasvata Manu, best of sages: when Manu sneezed, Brahmins, Ikshvaku was born as a son.
Ikshvaku had a hundred sons, giver of ample fees. Of them Vikukshi was the eldest; from being Vikukshi he was called Ayodhyan (unconquerable),
and, knower of supreme dharma, that lord became ruler of Ayodhya. His sons headed by Shakuni are remembered as five hundred.
The mighty protectors of the northern region were forty-eight, and in the southern direction likewise,
and others headed by Vashati, best of Brahmins, were protectors. Ikshvaku, on an Ashtaka day, commanded Vikukshi:
Mighty one, kill animals and bring meat for the shraddha. Assigned to the shraddha rite, while the shraddha was not yet performed,
he ate a hare, Brahmins, having gone hunting; hence "Shashada" (hare-eater). Abandoned by Ikshvaku on Vasishtha's word, the lord
— when Ikshvaku had passed away, Brahmins, Shashada became king. Shashada's heir was the valiant Kakutstha.
Kakutstha's son was Anenas, and Anenas's Prithu; Vishtarashva was Prithu's son, and from him Ardra was born.
Ardra's son was Yuvanashva, whose son was Shravasta, Brahmins; King Shravastaka was born, by whom Shravasti was built.
Shravasta's heir was the king Brihadashva; his son was Kuvalashva, a king of great righteousness,
who, having killed Dhundhu, obtained the name Dhundhumara.
Great sage, we wish to hear truly of the slaying of Dhundhu, by whose killing Kuvalashva came to be called Dhundhumara.
Kuvalashva had a hundred sons, excellent archers, all skilled in the sciences, strong and hard to withstand,
all righteous, sacrificers, givers of ample fees. His father Brihadashva appointed Kuvalashva to the kingdom.
Having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king entered the forest; as he was going, the Brahmin sage Uttanka stopped him.

You must provide protection, and you are able to do so; I cannot practise austerity without disturbance, king.
brahmapuran:7:61	Near my hermitage, on level desert ground, there is an ocean full of sand, called Uddalaka.
brahmapuran:7:62	Unslayable by the gods, huge in body and strong, a great being lies inside the earth, hidden beneath the sand.
brahmapuran:7:63	The Rakshasa Madhu's son, the great Asura named Dhundhu, lies there practising fierce austerity for the destruction of the world.
brahmapuran:7:64	At the end of the year he releases his breath; when he does, lord of men, the earth shakes there.
brahmapuran:7:65	By the wind of his breath great dust is raised, covering the sun's path, with earthquakes for seven days,
brahmapuran:7:66	with sparks, embers and smoke, most terrible. Because of it, dear, I cannot stay in my hermitage.
brahmapuran:7:67	Kill that huge being for the welfare of the worlds; the worlds will be at ease today when he is slain by you.
brahmapuran:7:68	For you alone, lord of the earth, are able to slay him, and a boon was given to me by Vishnu in an earlier yuga, king:
brahmapuran:7:69	'Whoever kills that great, terrible, mighty Asura, you will proclaim his splendour by the grant of a boon.'
brahmapuran:7:70	For the greatly radiant Dhundhu cannot be burned up by a small brilliance, lord of the earth, even in hundreds of yugas.
brahmapuran:7:71	His might is very great, hard for even the gods to approach. Thus addressed by the great-souled Uttanka, the royal sage gave his son Kuvalashva to him for slaying Dhundhu.
Revered one, I have laid down my weapons; this son of mine will be the Dhundhu-slayer, best of Brahmins, without doubt.
Having assigned his son to the killing of Dhundhu, the king of firm vows went to the mountain.
Kuvalashva, with a hundred sons, Brahmins, went with Uttanka for the destruction of Dhundhu.
Then the lord Vishnu with his power entered him, at Uttanka's behest, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds.
When that unassailable one had set out, a great sound arose in the sky: "This glorious one will today become Dhundhumara, unslayable."
The gods showered him with divine perfumes and garlands, and divine drums sounded, best of Brahmins.
That best of victors, mighty, went with his sons and had the ocean dug, the imperishable one hidden within the sand.
As his sons dug, Dhundhu, hidden in the sand, was reached, Brahmins, covering the western quarter.
With fire from his mouth, in anger, as though turning the worlds over, water flowed out with force like a great ocean at its rising.
Of the Moon's line, best of sages, great, filled with waves; of his hundred sons, all but three were burned by the Rakshasa.
Then the radiant king, of great splendour, approached the mighty Rakshasa Dhundhu, the destroyer of Dhundhu.
